The reproductive biology of Quingbo (Spinibarbus sinensis) shows several interesting features when compared with other cyprinids. Females first attain sexual maturity at a total length of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm], a size that corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of approximately 410 grams [Wwp = approximately 410 grams]. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of only 0.001 grams [Wwb = only 0.001 grams], a value computed from the egg diameter of the related species Barbus barbus. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs shortly after the completion of yolk sac resorption, marking the transition to the free-swimming larval phase. Interestingly, the maximum recorded reproductive output of Quingbo has been estimated from data on Barbus barbus, which suggests a peak daily egg production rate of 274 eggs per day [Ri = 274 eggs per day] when measured at a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C]; this equates to a female producing over 100,000 eggs annually under optimal thermal conditions.

The early life stages of Spinibarbus sinensis are characterized by rapid development, particularly during the incubation period. The age at birth, defined as the time from egg fertilisation to eclosion, is 18 days [ab = 18 days] when eggs are incubated at a stable temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively short embryonic period is typical of many warm-water cyprinids and allows larvae to begin exogenous feeding quickly. Following hatching, the prolarvae remain in a lecithotrophic state for a few days, absorbing their yolk reserves before the mouth opens. The pelagic larval phase is brief, and the fish undergo a pronounced larval metamorphosis, transitioning to a benthic juvenile lifestyle. The specific growth rate of these early juveniles has been measured under controlled laboratory conditions. At a body weight of 9.76 grams and a total length of 7.92 centimeters, individuals reared at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] exhibited a specific growth rate of 0.0083 per day , indicating a period of steady somatic increase during the post-metamorphic stage.

As Quingbo continues to grow, its body size increases substantially, eventually reaching an ultimate total length of 61 centimeters [Li = 61 centimeters] for the largest individuals. This maximum length is associated with an ultimate wet weight of 3800 grams [Wwi = 3800 grams], a relationship that follows a typical length-weight power function observed in the family Cyprinidae. The trajectory from a birth mass of just one milligram [Wwb = one milligram] to an adult mass of nearly four kilograms represents a dramatic increase of six orders of magnitude, highlighting the species' considerable growth potential. This pronounced size range allows Spinibarbus sinensis to exploit a variety of ecological niches across its life history; juveniles are often found in shallow, structured habitats where they feed on small invertebrates, while adults occupy deeper pools and are known to consume larger prey items including crustaceans and small fish. The species is also known to undertake seasonal migrations within river systems.

Longevity data for Spinibarbus sinensis, though limited, suggest a considerable lifespan for a cyprinid of its size. The life span has been estimated at 9125 days [am = 9125 days] based on individuals maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This extended lifespan is consistent with a relatively slow pace of life and is accompanied by a late age at sexual maturation, as females do not reach reproductive maturity until they achieve a total length of 30 centimeters [Lp = 30 centimeters]. The combination of a long life and delayed reproduction implies that individuals invest heavily in somatic growth before directing resources toward gamete production. Furthermore, the specific growth rate of 0.0083 per day  measured in juveniles at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is relatively modest compared to that of small, fast-maturing cyprinids, reinforcing the interpretation of a life history strategy oriented toward high adult survival and sustained growth over many years.

In addition to its remarkable longevity, Spinibarbus sinensis displays a high maximum reproductive rate that allows for substantial annual fecundity. At a water temperature of 22 °C [T = 22 °C], a female can produce approximately 274 eggs daily [Ri = approximately 274 eggs daily], which amounts to a theoretical yearly output exceeding 100,000 eggs. This elevated fecundity is likely an adaptation to compensate for high natural mortality during the early pelagic larval phases. The species also exhibits a notable disparity between the size at puberty and the ultimate adult size. Females reach sexual maturity at a total length of 30 cm [Lp = 30 cm] and a wet weight of 410 grams [Wwp = 410 grams], but they can continue to grow for many years afterward, eventually attaining the maximum body mass of 3800 grams [Wwi = 3800 grams]. This substantial post-pubertal growth, combined with the ability to produce large numbers of offspring annually, makes Spinibarbus sinensis a particularly resilient and highly fecund species within its native riverine ecosystems.
